newsitem.title: USA: Intel sees Q1 revs flat with Q4, up from year ago.
newsitem.headline: Intel sees Q1 revs flat with Q4, up from year ago.

text.p: Intel Corp said it expects first quarter 1997 revenues to be about flat with revenues of $6.4 billion in the just completed 1996 fourth quarter, but up from 1996's first quarter revenues of $4.64 billion.

Intel said its board of directors approved a two-for-one stock split to be effected as a stock distribution of one common share for each outstanding share, subject to stockholder approval of an increase in authorized shares at Intel's annual meeting on May 21, 1997.
Intel also said it expects gross margin percentage in the first quarter of 1997 to be flat to down from 63 percent in the fourth quarter.

The semiconductor maker also said it expects gross margin for all of 1997 at 60 percent plus or minus a few points. It said it still believes the gross margin percentage will be 50 percent plus or minus a few points over the long-term.
Additionally, it said first quarter expenses are expected to be about four percent to five percent percent higher than fourth quarter expenses of $1.2 billion.

Capital spending for 1997 is expected to be $4.5 billion versus $3.0 billion in 1996, it said. It said record unit shipments for its Pentium and Pentium Pro processors lifted 1996 revenue and earnings per share 29 percent and 44 percent, respectively, from 1995.

Intel reported fourth quarter revenues of $6.4 billion versus $4.6 billion a year ago. Net income rose to $1.9 billion from $867 million in the year ago fourth quarter while earnings per share rose to $2.13 from $0.98 a year earlier.
For the full year, revenue totaled $20.8 billion in 1996, up from $16.2 billion in 1995. Net income was $5.2 billion or $5.81 per share, up from $3.6 billion or $4.03 per share in 1995.
"Intel hit on all cylinders in 1996, the 25th anniversary of the introduction of the microprocessor," said Andrew Grove, president and chief executive officer.

"Fueling demand in 1996 were a number of factors including the continued growth of the Internet, the rapid penetration of PCs into emerging markets, especially in Asia, the beginnings of a corporate computing upgrade cycle and the increasing role the PC plays as a communications device," he said.
